headline_marked: [[Grok 4.5 uses 4x fewer tokens]] than Claude Opus 4.8 for similar coding, cutting costs.
headline: Grok 4.5 uses 4x fewer tokens than Claude Opus 4.8 for similar coding, cutting costs.
summary: xAI's Grok 4.5 delivers comparable coding quality to Claude Opus 4.8 but with significantly lower token usage, translating to substantial cost savings for developers.
details: xAI's Grok 4.5 aims to match Claude Opus 4.8 in coding performance while using roughly a quarter of the tokens. This efficiency is positioned as a major cost advantage for developers, potentially becoming a critical factor in AI adoption.

Grok 4.5, released on July 8, 2026, claims to use 4.2 times fewer output tokens than Opus 4.8 for equivalent coding tasks. Its base pricing is also lower, at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output, compared to Opus's $5 and $25 respectively.

Benchmarks show mixed results. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, Grok 4.5 scored 83.3% against Opus 4.8's 78.9%. However, Opus still outperforms Grok on SWE-Bench Pro, a more challenging test for fixing real open-source bugs.

A head-to-head test on a real Rust project revealed Grok's efficiency on larger tasks. While Opus won a small bug fix, Grok used approximately 197K tokens versus Opus's 954K for a refactor, and 603K versus 3.2 million for a feature build.

Cumulatively across three tasks, Grok used about 1.01 million tokens for $1.00, compared to Opus's 4.33 million tokens for $5.14. This demonstrates Opus using 4.3 times more tokens, closely aligning with xAI's advertised claims.

The test included caveats, such as Cursor's blended token counts, Opus running on a 'thinking tier' (potentially increasing token usage), and Grok benefiting from a 50% promo price. Even at full price, Grok's cost for the three jobs was about $2 versus Opus's $5.14.

For many everyday coding scenarios where output quality is similar, Grok's significant token and cost efficiency makes it a compelling choice, especially for large-scale development operations. The focus shifts from raw power to cost-per-job.

Opus retains an edge in quality for complex bug-fixing or when extra documentation and polish are highly valued, potentially justifying its higher cost. The emerging strategy involves matching the AI model to the specific task to optimize both performance and expenditure.

headline_marked: [[AMD reveals CPU roadmap through 2028]], confirming Zen 7 'Florence' for 2028 and Zen 8 'Ravenna' in development
headline: AMD reveals CPU roadmap through 2028, confirming Zen 7 'Florence' for 2028 and Zen 8 'Ravenna' in development
summary: AMD's long-term CPU strategy includes Zen 7 'Florence' arriving in 2028 with new AI compute extensions and diversified product families. The company also confirmed Zen 8 'Ravenna' is already in deep development for 2030.
details: AMD announced its long-term CPU roadmap at its Advancing AI event, detailing plans through Zen 8. The Zen 6 architecture, including the 256-core EPYC 9996 and Venice-X, was also a focus, with Venice-X slated for next year.

CEO Lisa Su confirmed Zen 7 'Florence' will debut in 2028, featuring next-gen Zen 7 cores and leading-edge process technology. Florence will also include new AI compute extensions and support the latest memory technologies.

Florence will not be a standalone processor family; it will be joined by the Ferrara AI host node and Faenza Agentic Sandbox. This approach aims to offer purpose-built CPUs for a wider range of AI workloads, moving beyond a single architecture for the entire server market.

Su also announced that the 8th Generation EPYC family, built on Zen 8 'Ravenna', is already deep in development. Ravenna is projected for a 2030 release, further extending AMD's predictable cadence for data center platforms.

On the accelerator side, AMD is developing its MI500-series Instinct products with next-generation HBM and larger scale-up domains. The company expects MI500 to deliver a significant generational leap, aiming for over 2,000 times higher inference throughput in four years.
AMD also confirmed its CDNA Next-based Instinct MI600 family is in development for 2028. The event also saw the launch of the MI455X GPU and teasers for the upcoming MI500X range, expected next year.
